candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XXII.1. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

The Akedah opens with 'And it came to pass after these things, that God did tempt Abraham'. Ephrem reads the temptation as PROBATIVE not deceptive — God already knows Abraham's heart; the test is FOR ABRAHAM, so that Abraham may know what was already in him. Tewahedo spiritual-formation theology (preserved in monastic ascetical texts) follows Ephrem: every trial reveals the soul TO ITSELF; God permits the testing so that the tested know their own depths.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XXII.8. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering'. Ephrem reads this verse as the most direct prophecy of the Crucifixion in the entire Torah: God will provide HIMSELF (i.e., God-incarnate) as the lamb. The substitution-of-ram (22:13) is a temporal stay; the ultimate lamb is the God-man on the Cross. Tewahedo Christology preserves Ephrem's reading: the ram caught in the thicket prefigures Christ's crown of thorns; Isaac unbound prefigures the empty tomb.

candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'In the mount of the Lord it shall be seen' (Jehovah-jireh). Ephrem reads Moriah as the SAME mountain (or its theological extension) that would become Calvary — the OT-NT typological geography is intentional. Tewahedo liturgical-theology preserves the Moriah-Calvary identification: the Tewahedo Anaphora explicitly recalls Moriah when commemorating the Crucifixion, treating the binding of Isaac as the OT side of a single redemptive event extending across two millennia.

Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos II.79 (c. 350 AD)

'And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed' — Athanasius marks en tō spermati sou (in thy seed, singular) as the ABRAHAMIC-SEED-AS-CHRIST anchor — explicitly so-interpreted by Paul at Gal 3:16 (ou legei kai tois spermasin... all' hōs eph' henos, kai tō spermati sou, hos estin Christos — 'he saith not and to seeds, as of many, but of one, and to thy seed, which is Christ'). The singular-not-plural sperma is the exegetical-key: the Abrahamic-blessing-to-all-nations is fulfilled in the one-Word-incarnate, not in Abraham's biological-descendants per se. Athanasius pairs Gen 22:18 with the Magi-narrative (Mt 2:1-12) and Acts 3:25 as the canonical Abrahamic-blessing-of-all-nations fulfillment-triplet.

Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

The Akedah opens with 'And it came to pass after these things, that God did tempt Abraham'. Ephrem reads the temptation as PROBATIVE not deceptive — God already knows Abraham's heart; the test is FOR ABRAHAM, so that Abraham may know what was already in him. Tewahedo spiritual-formation theology (preserved in monastic ascetical texts) follows Ephrem: every trial reveals the soul TO ITSELF; God permits the testing so that the tested know their own depths.

Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering'. Ephrem reads this verse as the most direct prophecy of the Crucifixion in the entire Torah: God will provide HIMSELF (i.e., God-incarnate) as the lamb. The substitution-of-ram (22:13) is a temporal stay; the ultimate lamb is the God-man on the Cross. Tewahedo Christology preserves Ephrem's reading: the ram caught in the thicket prefigures Christ's crown of thorns; Isaac unbound prefigures the empty tomb.

Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'In the mount of the Lord it shall be seen' (Jehovah-jireh). Ephrem reads Moriah as the SAME mountain (or its theological extension) that would become Calvary — the OT-NT typological geography is intentional. Tewahedo liturgical-theology preserves the Moriah-Calvary identification: the Tewahedo Anaphora explicitly recalls Moriah when commemorating the Crucifixion, treating the binding of Isaac as the OT side of a single redemptive event extending across two millennia.
